subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Brønsted–Lowry acids donate protons; bases accept them
Kw and the balance between H⁺ and OH⁻
Strong and weak, concentrated and dilute
Neutralization and the parents of a salt
The pH curve for a strong acid and strong base

questions.q:
Ammonia reacts with water:
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
Which species acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid in the forward reaction?
options: NH₃, as it gains a proton to form NH₄⁺
OH⁻, as it forms when H₂O loses a proton
None, as water is neutral and cannot donate
H₂O, as it donates a proton to NH₃
optionWhy: Gaining a proton is what a Brønsted–Lowry base does. NH₃ accepts H⁺, so it is the base; the acid is H₂O, which donates the proton.
OH⁻ is what is left after the acid has donated its proton: it is the conjugate base of H₂O. The acid is the reactant that loses H⁺, which is H₂O itself.
Water is amphiprotic. Here it donates H⁺ to NH₃, becoming OH⁻, so H₂O is the Brønsted–Lowry acid.
In the forward reaction H₂O loses H⁺ (becoming OH⁻) and NH₃ gains it (becoming NH₄⁺). The proton donor, H₂O, is the Brønsted–Lowry acid; NH₃ is the base.
questions.explain: In the forward reaction H₂O loses H⁺ (becoming OH⁻) and NH₃ gains it (becoming NH₄⁺). The proton donor, H₂O, is the Brønsted–Lowry acid; NH₃ is the base.

questions.q: Which pair of species is a conjugate acid–base pair?
options: H₃PO₄ and HPO₄²⁻
CH₃COOH and NH₃
H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻
HSO₄⁻ and SO₄⁻
optionWhy: H₃PO₄ and HPO₄²⁻ differ by two protons. A conjugate pair differs by one: the conjugate base of H₃PO₄ is H₂PO₄⁻.
CH₃COOH and NH₃ react with each other, but that makes them the acid and base of one reaction, not a conjugate pair. They do not differ by one proton; the pairs are CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ and NH₄⁺/NH₃.
The two species differ by exactly one proton: H₂PO₄⁻ − H⁺ = HPO₄²⁻. One H fewer and a charge one unit more negative is the signature of a conjugate pair.
Losing a proton (H⁺) lowers the charge by one. The conjugate base of HSO₄⁻ is SO₄²⁻; 'SO₄⁻' results from removing a hydrogen atom without changing the charge.
questions.explain: The two species differ by exactly one proton: H₂PO₄⁻ − H⁺ = HPO₄²⁻. One H fewer and a charge one unit more negative is the signature of a conjugate pair.

questions.q:
Dihydrogenphosphate ions react with ammonia:
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + NH₃(aq) ⇌ HPO₄²⁻(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq)
Which statement describes the role of H₂PO₄⁻ in the forward reaction?
options: It is an acid, as it gives up a proton to NH₃
It is a base, as it loses a proton to NH₃
It is a base, since negative ions only accept H⁺
It is both an acid and a base in this reaction
optionWhy: H₂PO₄⁻ becomes HPO₄²⁻: it loses H⁺, which NH₃ accepts. So in this reaction H₂PO₄⁻ is a Brønsted–Lowry acid. With a stronger acid such as H₃O⁺, the same ion would act as a base.
Losing a proton is the behaviour of an acid, not a base. H₂PO₄⁻ donates H⁺ to NH₃, so here it acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
Some anions contain an ionizable H and can donate it. H₂PO₄⁻ loses H⁺ in this reaction, so it acts as an acid, whatever its charge.
H₂PO₄⁻ is amphiprotic, meaning it can act as either, but in one reaction it plays one role. Here it only loses H⁺ (to NH₃), so it acts as an acid.
questions.explain: H₂PO₄⁻ becomes HPO₄²⁻: it loses H⁺, which NH₃ accepts. So in this reaction H₂PO₄⁻ is a Brønsted–Lowry acid. With a stronger acid such as H₃O⁺, the same ion would act as a base.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is diluted with distilled water to a total volume of 250 cm³. What is the pH of the diluted solution?
optionWhy: 1.00 is the pH of the original 0.100 mol dm⁻³ acid. After a 10-fold dilution [H⁺] is 10 times smaller, so the pH is 1 unit higher: 2.00.
Amount of HCl = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0250 dm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. In 0.250 dm³, [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³, so pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻²) = 2.00. A 10-fold dilution raises the pH by 1 unit.
This comes from 0.100 × 25.0 / 0.250 = 10.0 mol dm⁻³, using 25.0 cm³ as if it were 25.0 dm³. Converting gives 0.0250 dm³, [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ and pH 2.00.
4.61 is −ln(1.00 × 10⁻²), the natural logarithm. pH uses log₁₀: −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻²) = 2.00.
questions.explain: Amount of HCl = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0250 dm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. In 0.250 dm³, [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³, so pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻²) = 2.00. A 10-fold dilution raises the pH by 1 unit.
questions.working: n(HCl) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × (25.0/1000) dm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. [H⁺] = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.250 dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ (HCl is fully ionized). pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻²) = 2.00.

questions.q: Which statement about measuring the pH of an aqueous solution is correct?
options: Universal indicator is as precise as a pH meter.
A new pH meter reads accurately before it is calibrated.
A calibrated pH meter can give the pH to about 0.01 unit.
A reading of 7.00 shows a neutral solution at any temperature.
optionWhy: Universal indicator is read by matching a colour to a chart; each colour covers a range of pH and judging colour is subjective. It gives an estimate, typically to the nearest whole unit, not a precise value.
A pH meter must be calibrated with buffers of known pH before use, because the probe's response drifts with age and temperature. Without calibration its precise-looking readings can be inaccurate.
A pH meter (probe), calibrated with buffer solutions of known pH, gives a numerical reading, typically to 0.01 pH unit. Universal indicator only estimates pH, usually to the nearest whole unit.
Kw increases with temperature, so the pH of a neutral solution falls as the temperature rises. A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], which corresponds to pH 7.00 only at 298 K.
questions.explain: A pH meter (probe), calibrated with buffer solutions of known pH, gives a numerical reading, typically to 0.01 pH unit. Universal indicator only estimates pH, usually to the nearest whole unit.

questions.q: At 298 K, solution P has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and solution Q has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K. How does [OH⁻] in P compare with [OH⁻] in Q?
options: It is 100 times larger in P than in Q.
It is the same, as acid has no effect on [OH⁻].
Neither contains OH⁻ ions, as both are acidic.
It is 100 times smaller in P than in Q.
optionWhy: This assumes [OH⁻] = [H⁺] in every solution. That is true only in a neutral solution. Because [H⁺][OH⁻] = Kw is constant, the solution with 100 times more H⁺ has 100 times less OH⁻.
[H⁺] and [OH⁻] are linked by Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]. Adding acid shifts H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ to the left, lowering [OH⁻]: P has 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ and Q 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³.
Every aqueous solution contains both H⁺ and OH⁻. Acidic solutions simply have [H⁺] > [OH⁻]: here [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³ in P and 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ in Q.
[OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺]. P: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³; Q: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³. P has 100 times the [H⁺] of Q, so it has 1/100 of the [OH⁻].
questions.explain: [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺]. P: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³; Q: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³. P has 100 times the [H⁺] of Q, so it has 1/100 of the [OH⁻].

questions.q: A solution of nitric acid, HNO₃(aq), has a concentration of 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Which statement about this solution is correct?
options: It is a weak acid, as its concentration is low.
It contains mainly HNO₃ molecules with a few ions.
It is a dilute solution of an acid that is fully ionized.
It is neutral, as this much water neutralizes the acid.
optionWhy: Weak and dilute are different ideas. A low concentration makes the solution dilute; HNO₃ is still a strong acid because it is fully ionized.
That describes a weak acid. HNO₃ is strong: it is effectively completely ionized, so the solution contains H⁺(aq) and NO₃⁻(aq) with essentially no HNO₃ molecules.

HNO₃ is a strong acid, so it is fully ionized at this concentration: HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻, and [H⁺] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. At 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ the solution is dilute. Strength (extent of ionization) and concentration are independent.
Dilution spreads the H⁺ through more water but does not remove it. [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ (pH 3), far greater than [OH⁻], so the solution is acidic.
questions.explain: HNO₃ is a strong acid, so it is fully ionized at this concentration: HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻, and [H⁺] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. At 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ the solution is dilute. Strength (extent of ionization) and concentration are independent.

questions.q: Solution X is 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ KOH(aq). Solution Y is 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq). Which statement is correct?
options: NH₃ is the stronger base, as solution Y is more concentrated.
NH₃ is not a base, as its formula contains no OH group.
KOH is the stronger base, as it is fully ionized.
Both are strong bases, as both release OH⁻ ions in water.
optionWhy: Concentration and strength are different ideas. Y is more concentrated, but NH₃ is a weak base: fewer than 1 in 100 of its molecules have reacted with water. KOH is fully ionized, so it is the stronger base.
A Brønsted–Lowry base need not contain OH. The lone pair on the nitrogen of NH₃ accepts H⁺ from water, forming NH₄⁺ and OH⁻, so NH₃ is a (weak) base.

Strength is the extent of ionization, not concentration. KOH, a group 1 hydroxide, is fully ionized even in this dilute solution; NH₃ reacts only partly with water (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left), even at 2.0 mol dm⁻³.
Releasing OH⁻ makes both of them alkalis, not both strong. NH₃ produces OH⁻ only by reacting partly with water, and NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left. Only KOH is fully ionized.
questions.explain: Strength is the extent of ionization, not concentration. KOH, a group 1 hydroxide, is fully ionized even in this dilute solution; NH₃ reacts only partly with water (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left), even at 2.0 mol dm⁻³.

questions.q: Aqueous ethanoic acid is added to solid sodium carbonate until the reaction stops. What are the products of the reaction?
options: sodium ethanoate and water, with no gas
sodium ethanoate, hydrogen and carbon dioxide
none, as weak acids do not react with carbonates
sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
optionWhy: 'Acid + base → salt + water' is incomplete for carbonates. CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so carbon dioxide is also produced (the mixture fizzes).
Hydrogen is produced when an acid reacts with a reactive metal, not with a carbonate. The protons are accepted by CO₃²⁻, forming water and carbon dioxide.
Weak acids undergo all the typical acid reactions. As the carbonate removes H⁺, more ethanoic acid ionizes, so the reaction continues until one reactant is used up; vinegar fizzes with carbonates.
Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. The carbonate ion accepts two protons, forming H₂O and CO₂.
questions.explain: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. The carbonate ion accepts two protons, forming H₂O and CO₂.

questions.q: Methylammonium chloride, CH₃NH₃Cl, is a salt. Which statement about this salt is correct?
options: It forms from HCl and CH₃NH₂, with water as a second product.
It forms from HCl and CH₃NH₂, with no water produced.
Its parent base is CH₃NH₃OH, since a base must contain OH.
Its parent base is CH₃NH₃⁺, the cation present in the salt.
optionWhy: An amine, like ammonia, simply gains H⁺: CH₃NH₂ + H⁺ → CH₃NH₃⁺. No OH⁻ or O²⁻ is involved, so no water forms; the salt is the only product.
CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃Cl. The amine accepts a proton on the lone pair of its nitrogen atom, so the only product is the salt. Its parent acid is HCl and its parent base is the amine CH₃NH₂.

CH₃NH₃OH, written by analogy with 'NH₄OH', is not the parent base. An amine is a base because the lone pair on its nitrogen atom accepts H⁺, and it contains no OH: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃Cl. The parent base is CH₃NH₂.
CH₃NH₃⁺ is the ion in the salt, formed when the base gained a proton. Removing that proton gives the parent base, CH₃NH₂.
questions.explain: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃Cl. The amine accepts a proton on the lone pair of its nitrogen atom, so the only product is the salt. Its parent acid is HCl and its parent base is the amine CH₃NH₂.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is placed in a flask and 25.0 cm³ of distilled water is added. The mixture is then titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq). At what pH does the pH curve intercept the pH axis (0.00 cm³ of NaOH(aq) added)?
optionWhy: 1.00 is the pH of the undiluted 0.100 mol dm⁻³ acid. The added water doubles the volume, halving [H⁺] to 0.0500 mol dm⁻³, so the pH is 1.30.
3.00 is −ln(0.0500), the natural logarithm. pH uses log₁₀: −log₁₀(0.0500) = 1.30.
2.60 is −log₁₀(2.50 × 10⁻³), using the amount of HCl in mol as if it were a concentration. Dividing by the volume, 0.0500 dm³, gives [H⁺] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ and pH 1.30.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K until 50.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) has been added. Which statement about the pH curve is correct?
options: After 25.0 cm³ the pH stays at 7, as all the acid is neutralized.
The pH rises by an equal amount for each 1.00 cm³ of NaOH(aq) added.
The curve starts near pH 13, the pH of the NaOH(aq) added.
At 25.0 cm³ the pH is 7, as only NaCl(aq) and water are present.
optionWhy: Beyond 25.0 cm³ the added NaOH has no acid left to react with, so OH⁻ accumulates and the pH keeps rising, levelling off at about 12.5 by 50.0 cm³.
pH is logarithmic. Early additions remove only a small fraction of the H⁺, so the pH hardly changes; near 25.0 cm³ it jumps from about 3 to about 11 within 1 cm³.
The intercept is the pH of the solution in the flask before any titrant is added: 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl, pH 1.0. The curve rises towards, but does not reach, the pH of the NaOH(aq).
25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) contains the same amount as the HCl, so this is the equivalence point. The solution contains only NaCl and water, and a strong acid–strong base salt gives pH 7 at 298 K.
questions.explain: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) contains the same amount as the HCl, so this is the equivalence point. The solution contains only NaCl and water, and a strong acid–strong base salt gives pH 7 at 298 K.
